title: Programmable trained immunity with predictable protection and safety

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reliable way to give the innate immune system a useful, lasting change in how it responds to later threats. Trained immunity refers here to altered responses following an earlier exposure. Programming it would mean deliberately inducing a chosen response, measuring whether that state was established, predicting its duration and effects, and reversing it when necessary. The goal is controlled protection rather than simply increasing immune activity.

The supplied research frames this capability around changes in innate immune cells and their progenitors, with effects that may depend on cell lineage and tissue. Its central scientific question is how those changes determine the direction, persistence and safety of later responses. This is a coherent research target, but the supplied review had no captured source text with which to verify the broader biological claims or establish how much of this capability currently exists.

significance.text: Conditional significance: if a controllable trained state provided durable, clinically meaningful protection against unrelated infections, it could offer a way to prepare immune defenses against several threats through a common intervention. That would be a substantial preventive capability. The decisive benefit would be demonstrated protection in people, rather than the ability to produce molecular changes or stronger laboratory responses alone.

Predictability and reversibility would be central to that benefit. A useful intervention would need to produce an appropriate response in the relevant cells and tissues for a useful period, while allowing excessive or unwanted effects to be brought back under control. A persistent response would have limited value if its protective effects could not be separated from harmful inflammation.

The analogy to broad vaccination has limits: protection against several tested infections would establish a demonstrated range of benefit, not universal protection or a replacement for pathogen-specific immunity. Applications in cancer, sepsis or immune aging would remain separate possibilities requiring their own evidence. Neither trained-response markers nor an infection-protection result would by itself establish benefits in those settings.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a causal, predictive method for selecting and controlling a beneficial trained state. The research goal is to connect an intervention to molecular and cellular changes, then connect those changes to the direction and duration of later immune responses and to clinical outcomes. Observing that an exposure is followed by altered responses does not by itself provide rules for choosing a protective response in a new person or against a different threat.

Concrete barriers identified by the supplied research include determining which innate cell lineages carry the relevant changes, how progenitor changes contribute to persistence, and how effects differ across tissues. A programming method would also need measurements that distinguish an induced state from ordinary variation and predict whether that state is protective or harmful. The supplied material does not establish validated measurements or a general molecular programming code.

Reversal is a distinct engineering requirement. It would require a way to deliberately terminate or modify the induced state and evidence that doing so changes the relevant immune response. Allowing an effect to fade naturally would not establish controlled reversal. Safety also requires understanding when the same intervention could promote inflammatory or autoimmune harm, and whether its effects vary across populations. These are requirements of the proposed capability; the supplied evidence does not establish their present level of resolution.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes a human proof-of-concept result to Arts et al., “BCG Vaccination Protects against Experimental Viral Infection in Humans through the Induction of Cytokines Associated with Trained Immunity,” dated 10 January 2018, DOI 10.1016/j.chom.2017.12.010. It describes a randomized, placebo-controlled study in which BCG vaccination was associated with monocyte epigenetic changes and reduced viremia following challenge with an attenuated yellow-fever vaccine strain. This is the reported finding in the research input, rather than a result independently verified by the supplied review.

Taken as reported, the study provides a bounded example of an intervention associated with altered innate-cell markers and a virological outcome after an experimental challenge. An attenuated vaccine-strain challenge does not establish protection against multiple naturally acquired infections. The reported association between monocyte changes and reduced viremia also does not, by itself, establish a general causal programming method, predictable durability, controlled reversal or safety across populations.

The source index contains the paper’s PDF URL but no captured document content or saved artifacts. Consequently, the supplied review could not check the study design, findings, publication date, or the earlier page-specific attribution against the paper itself. No quantitative effect size or protection duration can be established from the supplied material. These access and extraction limits leave verification unresolved; they are not evidence that the reported result is false.

The supplied review also contains no bounded search record establishing subsequent developments through its stated freshness date of 1 November 2026. The 2018 report therefore cannot be treated as a complete account of the field at that date. The material does not establish that predictable, measurable and reversible trained immunity with broad clinical protection has been achieved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: establish causal molecular and cellular mechanisms that predict the direction and duration of trained responses, then use those mechanisms to deliberately induce and measure a chosen state in people. A convincing test would make predictions before outcomes are known and evaluate whether they hold in participants beyond those used to develop the method. These are proposed criteria, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Causal mechanisms predict induced trained-response direction and duration in people

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: controlled trials should show clinically meaningful protection against more than one unrelated infection, with prespecified clinical outcomes and follow-up sufficient to characterize how protection changes over time. The evidence should distinguish protection against natural infection or disease from effects confined to an experimental challenge. Successful finite trials would establish protection within the tested infections, populations and conditions, rather than literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Trials demonstrate clinically meaningful protection against multiple unrelated infections

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement and reversal demonstration: prespecify measures of the induced state and its functional consequences, then show that a deliberate reversal intervention changes both in the intended direction. Follow-up should distinguish reversal from spontaneous waning and determine whether unwanted effects recur or persist. This explicitly tests the measurement and reversibility goals that were present in the problem statement but incomplete in the earlier completion criteria.
completion_criteria.label: Deliberate reversal changes measured trained states and functional consequences

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: independent teams should reproduce the programming and protection results using a sufficiently specified intervention and measurement protocol. Trials should characterize inflammatory and autoimmune harms, variation across populations, and the circumstances in which the intervention fails or should not be used. Completion would require a defined benefit–risk profile and usable boundaries for duration, repeat administration and reversal, without assuming that one successful regimen generalizes to every setting.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce programming and protection with defined benefit–risk boundaries

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with IMM-01, “A general decoder for T-cell antigen recognition,” and IMM-03, “Vaccine design that reliably directs broadly protective antibody evolution”: all concern making immune protection more predictable. IMM-01 focuses on T-cell recognition, and IMM-03 on directing antibody evolution; IMM-12 focuses on programming trained innate responses. Success in one would not establish the recognition rules or protective mechanisms sought by the others.

Conceptual comparison with IMM-02, “A predictive, causal theory of whole immune responses,” and IMM-09, “In-body programming of immune cells as an inexpensive, scalable treatment”: IMM-12 could form a bounded component of a whole-immune-response theory and could overlap with in-body programming methods. Its distinctive requirement is control over the persistence, protective effects and reversibility of a trained innate state. A whole-system theory is broader, while an immune-cell programming platform would need separate evidence that it achieves this particular state safely.

Conceptual comparison with IMM-04, “Durable, antigen-specific reversal of established autoimmunity,” IMM-05, “Routine donor-specific transplant tolerance without lifelong immunosuppression,” and IMM-11, “Causal mechanisms that initiate the breakdown of self-tolerance”: these concepts intersect with IMM-12 through the need to avoid harmful immune responses. Reversing a trained state would not by itself establish antigen-specific reversal of autoimmunity, donor-specific tolerance, or a causal account of how self-tolerance first fails. Each remains a distinct objective.

Conceptual comparison with IMM-06, “General immune eradication of heterogeneous solid tumors,” IMM-07, “Immune-mediated, treatment-free control of established HIV infection,” and IMM-08, “Restoration of youthful immune competence in older adults”: trained immunity might eventually contribute to interventions in these areas, but the supplied material establishes no such benefit. Prevention of unrelated infections would not demonstrate tumor eradication, treatment-free control of established HIV, or restoration of youthful immune competence.

Conceptual comparison with IMM-10, “Real-time immune control of life-threatening systemic inflammation”: both require controlling immune activity and limiting inflammatory harm. IMM-12 concerns inducing and managing a persistent trained state; IMM-10 concerns controlling an acute, life-threatening process in real time. A reversible training method could be relevant to safety, but would not establish the speed or effectiveness required for acute systemic inflammation.

Conceptual comparison with IMM-13, “Predictive causal control of microbiome–immune interactions,” and IMM-14, “Causal, bidirectional control of neuroimmune circuits”: the overlap is the ambition to explain and deliberately control immune responses causally. Microbiome interactions and neuroimmune circuits could be relevant contexts for trained immunity, but no specific causal connection is established in the supplied evidence. Their control problems remain distinct from programming a durable innate response.

unresolved_issues: The Arts et al. paper’s design, findings, date, effect sizes and duration remain unverified against captured source content.
The supplied material does not establish the latest state of the field through 1 November 2026 or identify subsequent confirming, conflicting or extending studies.
The broader claims about innate-cell and progenitor memory, lineage effects, tissue effects and inflammatory risks lack inspected supporting artifacts in the supplied review.
No validated predictive measurements, causal programming rules or demonstrated human reversal method are established by the supplied evidence.
Appropriate infections, populations, follow-up periods, clinical endpoints and acceptable benefit–risk boundaries for the proposed demonstrations remain to be specified.

brief.title: Lasting infection protection that doctors can control
possible: People could prepare the body's first line of immune defense to protect against several unrelated infections. Doctors could choose a useful response, measure whether it took hold, predict how long it would last and reverse it when necessary.
why: A common treatment could give people lasting protection against several threats. Predictable control would help keep that protection useful while bringing excessive or unwanted immune responses under control.

sources.showed: This is a randomized trial comparing BCG vaccination with a placebo before an experimental challenge with a weakened yellow-fever vaccine virus.
sources.cited_for: It supports an early human test linking vaccination, altered immune cells and reduced virus in the blood.
sources.not_established: It does not establish protection against several naturally acquired infections, predictable duration or controlled reversal.

sources.who: Branko Cirovic, L Charlotte J de Bree and colleagues
sources.showed: BCG, a tuberculosis vaccine, caused lasting changes in gene activity in bone marrow cells that produce immune cells. Related changes appeared in circulating immune cells.
sources.quote: In this study, we show that BCG vaccination in healthy human volunteers induces a persistent transcriptional program connected to myeloid cell development and function within the hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) compartment in the bone marrow.
sources.cited_for: It connects lasting immune changes in people to the cells that replenish immune defenses.
sources.not_established: It does not establish rules for choosing a protective response or predicting its duration in a new person.

sources.showed: An interim trial analysis found fewer infections in older patients given BCG than in those given placebo. Most benefit involved respiratory infections thought to be viral.
sources.quote: No difference in the frequency of adverse effects was found.
sources.cited_for: It supports protection against naturally acquired infections in older patients, alongside altered immune responses.
sources.not_established: The interim result does not establish protection against several identified unrelated infections or safety across populations.

shown: Cirovic, de Bree and colleagues found lasting changes in bone marrow cells and circulating immune cells after BCG vaccination. These findings help explain how an earlier exposure can alter later immune responses, a process called trained immunity.

The ACTIVATE team went further toward practical protection: an interim randomized trial analysis found fewer infections in older patients after BCG vaccination. The strongest benefit involved respiratory infections thought to be viral.
missing: A method that deliberately produces a chosen immune response and predicts its duration in people.
Controlled trials establishing meaningful protection against several unrelated infections.
Measurements that predict protection or harm, plus a deliberate way to reverse the response.
Independent replication with clear limits for safety, repeat treatment and use across populations.

milestones.label: Chosen immune responses with predictable duration in people
milestones.explanation: A method would have to cause and measure a chosen response, then predict its direction and duration in new participants. This would turn biological understanding into reliable control.

milestones.label: Meaningful protection against several unrelated infections
milestones.explanation: Controlled trials would have to show meaningful protection against several unrelated infections and track how it changes over time. This would establish a tested range of benefit beyond experimental challenges.

milestones.label: Deliberate reversal changes immune state and response
milestones.explanation: A reversal treatment would have to change both the measured immune state and its effects, beyond natural fading. This would establish control over an unwanted response.

milestones.label: Independent replication with clear benefits and risks
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce programming and protection, defining harms and limits across populations, duration, repeat treatment and reversal. This would establish where treatment is useful and safe.

uncertain: Which immune cells and tissues determine whether a lasting response protects or harms?
Can measurements of an altered immune state reliably predict protection in an individual?
Which infections, populations and follow-up periods would establish an acceptable balance of protection and inflammatory or autoimmune harm?

page.title: Controlled induction and reversal of trained immunity
page.definition: Trained immunity is altered responsiveness of innate immune cells after an earlier stimulus has subsided. The capability is to induce a chosen protective state in people, predict its duration and response to an unrelated infection, and deliberately reverse it.

goal.need: Lower respiratory infections caused 2.7 million deaths worldwide in 2023. NIAID identifies trained innate immunity as a route to protection before pathogen-specific vaccines are available. Clinical protection requires direct testing: BRACE randomised 6,828 healthcare workers and found no reduction in severe febrile or respiratory illness over 12 months.

statements.body: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases
statements.quote: providing protection from severe disease early in a pandemic
statements.context: The Pandemic Preparedness Plan identifies this as the long-range objective of research on trained innate immunity, before pathogen-specific vaccines become available.

statements.quote: I propose that induction of trained immunity is an important novel approach to improved vaccination in the elderly.
is limited but tunable in duration, and is entirely reversible
statements.context: This describes the programme’s intended programmable gene-modulation effects. PREPARE addressed protective gene expression against threats including influenza; it did not establish a trained-immunity product criterion.

completion.title: A human regimen demonstrates predicted, reversible trained immunity and heterologous disease protection.
completion.criterion: A registered, controlled human programme meets prespecified endpoints for inducing innate immune memory, predicting its duration and heterologous protection in participants outside model development, and deliberately reversing the established state and its altered response. Independent investigators reproduce control and protection, and the regimen obtains regulatory approval for the demonstrated infectious-disease indication. Protocols specify prediction tolerances, follow-up, reversal endpoints and benefit–risk boundaries; no field-wide numerical cutoffs were found.
completion.set_by: Atlas proposal; no outside body located defines this combined capability. Regulatory approval uses the applicable product and indication requirements.
completion.basis: NIAID’s plan, TRAIN-OLD, DARPA PREPARE, the trained-immunity development roadmap, FDA vaccine guidance and BCG/MV130 trial documents supplied no end-to-end test combining prediction, protection and active reversal. This is an Atlas composite, not an agency standard. The roadmap identifies uncertainties about duration and reversibility. Approval establishes clinical benefit–risk for an indication; it cannot by itself establish programmable control.

milestones.title: Trained human monocytes increase cytokine release after 24-hour priming and 6 days of rest.
milestones.criterion: In Bekkering et al.’s published assay, expose human monocytes to a training stimulus for 24 hours, wash, rest for 6 days, and rechallenge with an unrelated microbial stimulus for 24 hours. Demonstrate increased cytokine release versus medium-trained controls using the specified paired analysis and two-sided p < 0.05. The 2016 experiments reported increased IL-6 and TNF-α responses after β-glucan or BCG training, with n = 6. This establishes a laboratory phenotype, not protection.
milestones.set_by: Bekkering and colleagues, published human-monocyte training protocol and statistical criterion; these timings are assay conditions, not a universal protection threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: A two-sided P value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

milestones.title: Preclinical studies establish heterologous protection and support first human dosing.
milestones.criterion: Laboratory and animal data must support a regulator’s finding that human dosing is reasonably safe. A model-specific protection result was published in 2019: β-glucan given 7 days before Leishmania braziliensis challenge reduced tissue parasite burden at 8 weeks in human-IL-32γ-transgenic mice, with 6 mice/group and p < 0.05. Wild-type mice did not benefit, and transgenic lesions initially enlarged. This experiment demonstrated protection in that model; it did not establish regulatory safety clearance.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Vaccine Development – 101, preclinical assessment before human testing; the protection endpoint comes from dos Santos et al.’s published mouse-challenge protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: reasonably safe for testing of the vaccine to move forward in people.

milestones.title: BCG induces bone-marrow and circulating innate-cell changes persisting 90 days in people.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate molecular and functional changes at the human study’s 90-day sampling endpoint. Cirovic, de Bree and colleagues randomised 20 healthy BCG-naive adults aged 18–50 years to intradermal BCG, 0.1 mL, or placebo: 15 and 5 participants respectively. The 2020 publication reported persistent transcriptional changes in bone-marrow blood-cell progenitors, altered monocyte chromatin accessibility and increased responses to unrelated stimulation. These observations establish persistence at the sampled time, not an individually predicted duration.
milestones.set_by: Cirovic, de Bree and colleagues, published randomised human study protocol; 90 days is its observation endpoint, not a field-wide durability requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: Blood was drawn before, two weeks after and three months after vaccination.

milestones.title: BCG lowers day-5 yellow-fever vaccine viraemia versus placebo in a human challenge.
milestones.criterion: Meet the published challenge endpoint of lower circulating vaccine-strain yellow-fever virus at day 5, measured by PCR, with p < 0.05 by Mann–Whitney U test. Arts et al. randomised 30 men aged 19–37 years to BCG or placebo, followed one month later by yellow-fever vaccination. The paper published on 10 January 2018 reported reduced viraemia. Its methods exclude one BCG recipient from yellow-fever analyses. An attenuated-virus challenge does not establish prevention of naturally acquired disease.
milestones.set_by: Arts and colleagues, published controlled human challenge protocol, Figure 3 and methods.

milestones.title: A trained state’s duration is predicted and its established response is actively reversed in people.
milestones.criterion: In a controlled human study, a predeclared model predicts the response’s magnitude and duration in new participants. An intervention administered after training is established returns specified molecular and rechallenge-response endpoints to a protocol-defined untrained range, beyond changes in untreated trained controls. Blocking initial induction and spontaneous waning do not satisfy this proposed test. No qualifying human result or published numerical acceptance limits were located.
milestones.set_by: Atlas proposal: searches of the trained-immunity roadmap, agency programmes and clinical-trial literature did not locate a human prediction-and-reversal acceptance criterion.

milestones.title: A phase 3 trial demonstrates heterologous disease protection with acceptable safety.
milestones.criterion: Meet a phase 3 protocol’s clinical efficacy and safety criteria. ACTIVATE (2020; 150 completers): infections occurred in 18/72 BCG versus 33/78 placebo recipients; p = 0.039 exceeded interim α = 0.0054. BRACE (2024; n = 6,828): the 12-month severe-illness risk difference was +0.6 percentage points (95% CI −1.3 to +2.5). MV130 (2026; n = 198) reduced COPD exacerbations from 2.68 to 1.87/person-year over 18 months; that endpoint did not establish protection against a specified unrelated pathogen or programmed control.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Vaccine Development – 101, phase 3 clinical effectiveness and safety assessment; individual trial protocols determine their indication-specific endpoints.
milestones.threshold_quote: whether the vaccine reduces the incidence of disease.

not_found: No outside body’s completion test combining predicted duration, heterologous protection and deliberate reversal was located.
No human demonstration meeting the proposed prediction-and-reversal milestone was located.
The yellow-fever analysis sample-size discrepancy between the Arts figure legend and methods could not be resolved.
ClinicalTrials.gov study pages did not expose their outcome records; trial endpoints here come from opened publications.

results.finding: In 20 volunteers, BCG was associated with bone-marrow and circulating innate-cell changes at 90 days.
results.detail: The study assigned 15 participants to BCG and 5 to placebo. It reported progenitor transcriptional changes, altered monocyte chromatin accessibility, and increased responses to unrelated stimulation.
results.quote:
In this study, we demonstrate that human
in vivo
BCG vaccination induces sustained transcriptomic changes in HSPCs of healthy individuals, changes that are accompanied by persistent increase of innate immune cells responsiveness to heterologous stimuli.

results.finding: Baseline CCL23 correlated with the day-14 response after BCG; 15 volunteers received BCG, but the correlation sample size is unspecified.
results.detail: The correlation was not a predeclared model validated in new participants and did not predict duration. AAT was given during ex vivo training, so its inhibitory effect did not demonstrate reversal of an established response in people.

results.finding: Phase III BCG trial (n=141): COVID-19 disease 23.7% vs 41.7% placebo (p=0.023); no moderate/severe BCG-related adverse events.
results.detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase III in BCG-naive US adults with type 1 diabetes; multi-dose Tokyo-174 BCG. Co-primary outcomes were COVID-19 disease and all infectious diseases; p<0.05 and p<0.0001 respectively. Safety: no moderate/severe AEs related to BCG. This is heterologous protection in a specific population, not regulatory approval.
results.quote: COVID-19 disease occurred in 22 of 93 participants in the BCG group (23.7%) and in 20 out of 48 participants in the placebo group (41.7%) ( Figure 2 ).
